model.comments: High effort Claude Fable 5.1. Thinking is always on for Fable; depth is controlled by Anthropic's output_config.effort, which OpenRouter sets from reasoning.effort (its verbosity field maps to the same native field, so this equals the older opus-4.x verbosity convention).

prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Amazons on a 6x6 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(board) -> str: ... ``` # State Representation - `board` is a 6x6 numpy array (dtype can be int). - Cell values: - - `0` = empty square - - `1` = your amazon - - `2` = opponent amazon - - `-1` = arrow / blocked square - You may assume the board is valid. # Action / Return Format - Return a single move string formatted exactly as: `"from_row,from_col:to_row,to_col:arrow_row,arrow_col"`. - All coordinates are 0-indexed with `row,col` in `0..5`. - Example (syntax only): `"0,1:2,3:3,3"` moves from (0,1) to (2,3) then shoots an arrow to (3,3). - Your move must be legal and consists of two parts: - - Move one of your amazons (`board == 1`) from `from` to `to`. - - From the landing square `to`, shoot an arrow to `arrow`. - Movement rules (queen-like) for both the amazon move and arrow shot: - - Any positive number of squares in a straight line, orthogonally or diagonally. - - The path must be unobstructed and may not cross or land on any non-empty square. - Blockers are: your amazons (`1`), opponent amazons (`2`), and arrows (`-1`). - Additional legality constraints: - - `from` must contain your amazon (`board[from] == 1`). - - `to` must be empty in the original position (`board[to] == 0`). - - For the arrow shot, treat the amazon as having moved to `to` and vacated `from`. - - `arrow` must be empty after the move; it may pass through the vacated `from` square if unobstructed. - Terminal condition: - - The last player who can make any legal move wins. - - The environment should not call `policy` when you have no legal move, but your policy must still be robust. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm working out the approach for an Amazons policy on a 6x6 board: alpha-beta search with iterative deepening under a time budget, using an evaluation based on queen-move territory distances and mobility differences, plus generating legal moves (queen moves followed by arrow shots) for each amazon.

Rough math suggests each amazon could have around 100 candidate moves once arrow placements are factored in, meaning a full depth-2 search could balloon to hundreds of thousands of evaluations—too slow for Python in one second unless I tighten the evaluation cost and rely on move ordering. I'm estimating that a fast queen-distance BFS eval might cost around 200 microseconds, giving me roughly 4000 evaluations in my time budget, which comfortably covers depth 1 and a partial depth 2 with good alpha-beta pruning and ordering.

One practical way to keep depth 2 affordable is to first score all root moves cheaply at depth 1, then only expand the most promising candidates further rather than searching every move at full depth.

I think iterative deepening alpha-beta with move ordering by cheap heuristics makes sense here—using the previous depth-1 eval to order root moves and a fast heuristic to order opponent replies, keeping a depth-1 result always available as a fallback under time pressure.

For the endgame case where territories split into separate regions, I can approximate move count within each region using the queen-distance territory count rather than computing exact optimal play. I'll define the evaluation as a weighted sum: queen-territory difference weighted heaviest, king-territory difference as a smaller factor, and mobility difference (counting queen-reachable empty squares per amazon) as a minor tiebreaker.

I'm also noting that a trapped amazon with zero mobility effectively loses its territory automatically, since the BFS from it won't reach anywhere, so that's already handled correctly. Now I'm setting up the board representation and precomputing the movement rays for each square.

Writing ray precomputation code...

Now I'm implementing the move generator, which finds every legal amazon move and arrow placement by walking rays from each occupied square.

Next I'm setting up a BFS-based territory evaluation that computes queen-move distances from each player's pieces to every square on the board.

For scoring, I'm counting squares closer to each player as territory points, with ties handled by favoring whoever moves next, following standard Amazons scoring conventions.

Actually working through the equal-territory case more carefully: if both sides have k reachable squares and it's my turn, I run out first and lose, so equal territory favors whoever isn't to move. I'll fold that tie-break into the eval and rely on exact terminal detection during search — if a side has no legal moves, that's an immediate loss for them. Now I'm setting up a negamax framework with alpha-beta pruning from the perspective of the side to move.

Generating the full move list at every leaf node is too expensive, so I want a cheap way to test if a player has any move at all: since an amazon can always move to any adjacent empty square and then shoot back at its own vacated origin, having a move is equivalent to having at least one amazon with an empty adjacent square.

For the mobility term, I'll piggyback on the BFS territory computation and use the count of empty squares reachable at distance one as a rough weight, maybe around 0.15, added to the territory score which ranges roughly -36 to 36. For move ordering at non-leaf nodes, I want a cheap heuristic like prioritizing arrow placements near opponent amazons or that shrink opponent mobility, without doing a full eval.

Ordering leaves still matters for cutoff speed, so I could score moves by counting how many of my amazons are adjacent to the arrow or destination square using precomputed neighbor lists—cheap enough per node given eval cost dominates. I'm also considering narrowing the branching at depth-2 nodes by only exploring a subset of moves rather than all of them.

I'll stick with full-width alpha-beta at depth 2 with a time cutoff, using iterative deepening: if the search is interrupted, I keep the best move from the current iteration if at least one root move fully completed and improved on the previous best, otherwise fall back to the prior iteration's result, since root moves are ordered by previous evaluations.

For timing, I'll budget around 0.55s of the 1s limit to stay safe on potentially slower hardware, checking elapsed time via perf_counter at every node since that overhead is negligible compared to leaf evaluation cost.

For the endgame case where territory is fully divided, I want to be more precise about counting reachable squares rather than just approximating, since the search will refine details near the end anyway. I'm also handling the tie-break rule for equal distances by favoring the player to move, and writing the evaluation function that scores territory by comparing each empty square's distance to both players.

Skipping king-distance weighting for simplicity, and adding a mobility term based on how many squares each amazon can reach as a queen, treating trapped amazons as zero-mobility. Now I'm writing the main policy function that generates moves and starts timing the search.

If no legal moves exist, I return a placeholder move for validity. Otherwise I score each move at depth 1 by applying it and negating the opponent's evaluation, sort the scored moves best-first, and pick the top one before continuing into iterative deepening for greater depth. I'm folding terminal detection into the negamax search itself: if the current player has no moves, that position gets a large negative score scaled by depth so earlier mates are preferred.

Now I'm designing move ordering and the iterative deepening loop: root moves get reordered using scores from the previous depth, each depth is explored with alpha-beta and a time cutoff that raises an exception caught at the top level, moves are applied and undone by toggling the from/to/arrow cells directly, and inner-node ordering uses a heuristic weighting how many enemy amazons are adjacent to the arrow and king-square.

Writing BFS mobility function...

Rough timing suggests each move evaluation costs about 0.3ms, meaning depth-1 search could handle 2000+ evaluations in the 0.6s budget while depth-2 with alpha-beta pruning might need 1000-3000, putting it right at the edge of feasibility, especially early in the game when move counts are highest. I'm considering cheaper evaluation heuristics for depth-2 leaf nodes or trimming the opponent reply set to keep things fast.

With good move ordering, refutations get found quickly, so I want a better cheap heuristic for ranking opponent replies — weighting arrow and destination proximity to opponent amazons more heavily since those moves tend to cut into my territory most. I could also borrow the killer-move idea to reuse effective refuting moves across similar positions.

I'll implement per-depth killer moves: store the last cutoff-causing move at each depth and try it first next time, since sibling nodes differ only by my move and often share a good refutation—checking membership in the move list is cheap enough to do once per node. I'll also order root moves using scores from the previous iterative-deepening pass, and add a time check inside the depth-1 pass itself, budgeting around 0.6s total for safety given unknown overhead on the 1-second target.

If time runs out during depth-1, I'll just fall back to the best move found so far. I also need a helper that checks whether a given side still has any legal move by scanning board squares for that player's pieces and checking adjacent empty neighbors, and I want to unify the "no moves" terminal case so the root loop calls the same negamax logic that handles it internally rather than duplicating that check.

Now I'm writing the negamax function with time checks, terminal detection when a side has no moves, alpha-beta pruning, and killer move tracking on cutoffs. I'm weighing how often to check the timer against overhead, and estimating that move ordering by adjacency counts at inner nodes costs roughly as much as evaluating a few extra positions, which seems acceptable.

I'm also planning iterative deepening at the root: keep increasing search depth while time permits, stopping early if a forced win is found, and setting up the loop that will track scores per root move.

Refining root-level move ordering...

On timeout, cur_best comes from moves fully evaluated at this depth—the first (previous best) is always complete, and later ones only if they raised alpha, so this is a reasonable standard fallback even though sorting by partial bounds is approximate. I'm also considering minor eval tweaks like secure-territory weighting but deciding to skip more elaborate distance metrics for now.

I need to handle board input by flattening the numpy array into a flat list of ints, then format the output move as coordinate strings, with a dummy fallback move in case none exist (though the environment shouldn't call us then). Now I'm setting up constants for board size, movement directions, and precomputed rays/neighbors before writing the full solution...

Writing move generation and ray-casting logic...

Still writing distance/mobility function...

I'm weighing whether to add a king-distance territory term but decide it's not worth another BFS pass right now. For the killer move table, I'll key it by search depth.

For move ordering, I want to score each move by how many enemy amazon-adjacent squares the arrow and destination touch, giving killer moves a large bonus so they get tried first. I realize I can precompute adjacency counts to enemy queens for all 36 squares once, then reuse that lookup for scoring every move instead of recomputing neighbors each time.

I'm now settling on a time budget around 0.6 seconds to be safe against slower arena hardware, and estimating whether depth-2 search is feasible given roughly 300 legal moves per turn in the opening — depth-1 evaluation should take about 0.1s, while depth-2 with killer move ordering is borderline around 0.5s, so I'll need to rely on partial results if it doesn't finish.

I'll keep the leaf evaluation simple, check the time budget periodically using a node counter, and use a global deadline variable to control cutoffs cleanly.
